interviewQuestions.question: How would you rotate an array to the right by k in O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd use the reversal trick: reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n-k elements.

First I reduce k with `k %= n`, since a rotation by n is a full cycle back to the start — skipping this either crashes on an out-of-range slice or wastes a redundant full pass.

The mechanism: reversing the entire array puts everything in reverse order, which is almost the rotated order except the two segments (what should be the front and the back) are each individually backwards. Reversing each segment on its own un-reverses just that piece, landing every element in its correct rotated position. Concretely, rotating `[1,2,3,4,5,6,7]` right by 3: full reverse gives `[7,6,5,4,3,2,1]`, reversing the first 3 gives `[5,6,7,4,3,2,1]`, reversing the last 4 gives the correct `[5,6,7,1,2,3,4]`.

Each of the three reversals reuses the same two-pointer swap-from-both-ends routine and is O(n); doing it three times is still O(n) overall, and the only extra memory is a couple of index variables — O(1) space.

I'd mention cyclic replacement as the alternative O(1)-space approach, but default to the reversal trick because it's three independent, easy-to-verify passes rather than one pass whose correctness depends on correctly handling multiple cycles.

**Testing:** whether you can produce a genuinely O(1)-space solution rather than the array-slicing one-liner that looks in-place but isn't.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: What's wrong with rotated = arr[k:] + arr[:k] if the interviewer asked for an in-place, O(1)-space solution?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It's the answer that looks in-place because it reuses the variable name, but isn't — the actual memory cost is O(n), not O(1).

Breaking it down: `arr[k:]` allocates a new list holding n-k elements; `arr[:k]` allocates a second new list holding k elements; the `+` concatenation allocates a *third* list combining both. All of that happens before anything gets assigned back to `rotated` (or even to `arr`, if you reassign it). "In-place" describes the algorithm's peak extra memory during execution, not whether the final result lands back in a variable with a familiar name — and this solution's peak extra memory is a full copy of the array, twice over.

The tell to watch for in any solution, your own or someone else's: any full-size temporary — a new list, a `.copy()`, a sliced sublist — means the space bound has already failed, regardless of what happens to the result afterward.

The actual in-place fix is the reversal trick or cyclic replacement, both of which mutate `arr`'s existing backing storage directly and never materialize a second full-size array at any point. I'd catch this in code review by asking "what's the largest single allocation this makes," which surfaces the hidden copy immediately.

**Testing:** whether you understand what in-place actually measures, rather than pattern-matching on syntax that looks minimal.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Correctness

interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through cyclic replacement for array rotation, and when would you prefer it over the reversal trick?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Cyclic replacement rotates by moving each element directly to its final destination index, rather than reversing segments. For a right rotation by k, the element at index i belongs at `(i + k) % n`. I hold the value at index 0, move whatever's currently at its destination out first — saving it — drop the held value in, and keep following that chain of displaced values until it loops back to index 0, completing one cycle.

The catch: that first cycle only covers every index when `gcd(n, k) == 1`. Whenever `gcd(n, k) > 1`, the indices split into that many separate cycles, and you need to detect and start a new cycle from an index not yet visited. Getting this wrong — assuming one cycle always suffices — is the classic live-coding bug with this technique.

Both cyclic replacement and the reversal trick hit O(n) time, O(1) space, so the choice is about robustness versus efficiency of writes, not asymptotics. I'd default to the reversal trick in an interview — three independent, easy-to-verify passes are much harder to get subtly wrong under pressure than correctly enumerating cycles. I'd reach for cyclic replacement specifically if minimizing total element writes actually mattered, e.g. rotating a huge array where write bandwidth (not just complexity class) is the binding constraint, since it does exactly n writes total versus three full passes' worth of swaps.

**Testing:** whether you can implement the trickier of the two O(1)-space techniques correctly, including its cycle-counting edge case.

interviewQuestions.question: You add an in-place rotation to a shared utility function, and a downstream service starts returning subtly wrong results for unrelated requests. How would you explain that?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My first hypothesis: the array being rotated isn't exclusively owned by the function that rotated it — it's a shared reference, and the in-place mutation is visible to every other holder of that reference.

In-place algorithms are an optimization on the assumption that the caller either owns the array exclusively or has explicitly agreed the input can be modified. If the array is actually a cached result, a memoized computation, or a view backed by the same memory as a larger structure, then rotating it in place doesn't just rotate "my copy" — there is no copy. Every other reader sees the mutated order from that point forward, silently, with no exception raised anywhere. This is a real production bug class, and it's especially nasty because the symptom shows up far from the actual mutation — a request that never touched the rotation code returns wrong data because it read the same shared array afterward.

How I'd confirm it: check whether the array passed to the rotation function is a reference to something stored elsewhere — a class attribute, a module-level cache, an object returned from an earlier call rather than freshly constructed — versus something newly allocated per request.

The fix is either to make the function copy defensively before mutating (giving up the O(1)-space win for correctness), or to document and enforce — via ownership convention, or a wrapper type — that callers must pass an array they're prepared to have mutated. I'd pick the defensive copy by default in shared utility code; the O(1)-space optimization is only worth keeping where the caller genuinely controls the array's lifetime.

**Testing:** whether you connect an algorithmic space-complexity win to a real aliasing bug in production code, not just interview-puzzle correctness.
